title: An Indian Worker Died in Ukraine's Biggest Drone Strike on Moscow — and India's War Tightrope Just Got Harder to Walk
excerpt: One killed, three injured as over 1,000 Ukrainian drones hit Russia. For 20,000 Indians working there, the conflict is no longer someone else's war.
body:
An Indian worker was killed and three others injured when Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery complex in Moscow's outskirts on May 17, making him one of at least four fatalities in what Russia described as the largest aerial assault on the capital region in over a year.

## What Happened

Ukraine launched a massive wave of over 1,000 drones at Russian territory in a 24-hour blitz, with 81 shot down over the Moscow region alone. The strikes targeted energy infrastructure, including oil refineries and fuel depots — part of Kyiv's stated strategy of degrading Russia's export revenues and forcing the war's economic costs onto Moscow's civilian population.

The Indian national, whose identity has not been publicly released, was working at or near one of the targeted facilities. Three other Indian workers sustained injuries. The Indian Embassy in Moscow confirmed the casualties within hours and said it was "providing all possible assistance," including coordinating hospital care and liaising with Russian authorities.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, responding to the strikes, called them "entirely justified" as retaliation for Russia's sustained bombardment of Ukrainian cities. He made no specific mention of the Indian casualty but defended the targeting of energy infrastructure as a legitimate act of war.

## India's Tightrope

The death puts India's carefully calibrated position on the Russia-Ukraine war back under the spotlight. New Delhi has consistently called for dialogue and a ceasefire while maintaining close ties with Moscow — India remains one of Russia's largest oil buyers and a major defence-equipment customer. At the same time, India has deepened engagement with Ukraine, with PM Modi visiting Kyiv in 2024 in a symbolic gesture that Zelenskyy publicly welcomed.

India's Ministry of External Affairs has not issued a formal statement beyond the Embassy's confirmation. But behind the scenes, the incident is likely to intensify diplomatic conversations about the safety of Indian nationals in conflict zones. An estimated 15,000–20,000 Indians live and work in Russia, many in construction, IT, and energy-sector roles. During the early days of the 2022 invasion, India evacuated thousands of students from Ukraine; now the risk has migrated to the other side of the front line.

## A Pattern of Civilian Casualties

The Moscow drone attack fits a grim escalatory pattern. Both Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted civilian and dual-use infrastructure deep behind enemy lines. Russia's missile strikes on Ukrainian cities have killed thousands; Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries and logistics hubs has intensified since late 2025, with tacit Western acquiescence.

For Indian workers caught in the middle — often employed by Russian energy firms or subcontractors — the risk calculus has shifted. Unlike diplomats or students, blue-collar workers are less likely to be covered by organised evacuation protocols. Community leaders in Moscow's small Indian diaspora have called for the Embassy to conduct a formal risk assessment and issue updated advisories.

## The Diaspora Response

Indian social media lit up with anger and grief after the news broke. Families of Indians working in Russia expressed frustration at the lack of prior warning. "We hear about the war on TV, but nobody tells you your son's workplace could be a target," said one relative quoted by Indian media.

The incident also revived calls from opposition politicians for the government to take a clearer stance on the conflict. "You cannot buy discounted oil from Russia and pretend the war does not exist," tweeted a prominent Congress leader, a line that captured the uncomfortable bargain at the heart of India's foreign policy.

## What Comes Next

The Indian Embassy has set up a dedicated helpline for Indian nationals in Russia and is urging all citizens to register with the Embassy's database. For families back home — in Gujarat, Punjab, Kerala, and beyond — the death is a stark reminder that globalisation's rewards come with risks that no government policy can fully hedge.

With the war showing no signs of ending and drone technology making every industrial site a potential target, the question for India is no longer theoretical: how do you protect your people when they are scattered across a war zone, working jobs that keep two economies running?
